reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes lending BNB, TRX, ETH, or similar cryptocurrency through Fintoch with a stated 1% daily return and directs viewers to contact the speaker, join an investor or business-builder team, and pursue the platform opportunity. The withdrawal screen also shows access to a displayed amount subject to a 5% service fee. The material does not establish a completed withdrawal, victim loss, or that the stated returns were received, and it includes a disclaimer that nothing can be guaranteed.

citations.quote: if you actually loaned out a crypto currency like BNB, to generate the 1% profit per day, how do you check your income?
Next to it there's an arrow down, click on it, and there you see the bnb.
1 January 2023 i started my investment with FINTOCH and benefitted greatly gaining a 6 figure profit in just 2 months.

opening.argument: Judge, the stated return deserves scrutiny, but it should be read alongside the creator's explicit warning to viewers: “nothing can be guaranteed” and there are “uncertainty and risks.” The description tells viewers to do their own research and limit any investment to disposable income. Those qualifications matter when deciding whether this is deceptive solicitation or a creator discussing a risky activity they personally undertook. The video itself answers a practical question about locating income in the app, rather than promising that a viewer will achieve the creator's result.

citations.quote: As you know nothing can be guaranteed in this world, so in all that we do, there will be certain level of uncertainty and risks.
do please do your own research and analysis before you embark on your own wealth creation journey. Invest ONLY the DISPOSABLE portion of your DISPOSABLE INCOME.
how do you check your income?

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited “1% profit per day” establishes what the speaker says the lending activity generates, not that the speaker promises every viewer a guaranteed payout. The cited personal profit claim is an account of the creator's own experience, not proof that viewers will receive the same amount. The opening acknowledges that neither a completed withdrawal nor receipt of the stated returns is established. The explicit risk warning is therefore material context, even if it does not validate the platform.

citations.quote: if you actually loaned out a crypto currency like BNB, to generate the 1% profit per day, how do you check your income?
These videos are just to share my personal experience and financial journey and also my learnings.
As you know nothing can be guaranteed in this world

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The disclaimer does not change what the video promotes. The speaker describes lending cryptocurrency “to generate the 1% profit per day,” while the description reports a six-figure personal profit and offers to guide people who join the creator's team. Those elements invite viewers toward an investment opportunity; warning them to research it does not establish that the advertised return is real or reliably obtainable.

citations.quote: if you actually loaned out a crypto currency like BNB, to generate the 1% profit per day
benefitted greatly gaining a 6 figure profit in just 2 months.
Only if you are sincere to join my team of investors and business builders then connect with me and I will guide you how.

opening.argument: The immediate task here is operational: a viewer asks where to find the income associated with lending BNB, and the speaker walks through the app's Lending and Profit sections. The explanation addresses a specific point of confusion: BNB does not appear where the viewer first expects it, so the speaker identifies the dropdown that reveals it. That is a concrete navigation demonstration, not evidence that anyone watching has invested or withdrawn money. The daily-return claim warrants caution, but it is not the whole content of this particular video.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites the daily-return line but underweights the question that follows it: “how do you check your income?” The speaker then demonstrates a dropdown, and the displayed BNB balance supports that the tutorial is about finding an entry in an interface. Neither that balance nor the withdrawal screen proves a completed payout. The invitation in the description is promotional context, but it does not erase the video’s specific instructional purpose.

citations.quote: how do you check your income?
Next to it there's an arrow down, click on it, and there you see the bnb.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Showing viewers where to find a balance is instructional, but the instruction serves the investment pitch. The speaker frames lending BNB as generating “1% profit per day” and calls the displayed BNB “your profits.” The description then invites people to join the creator's investor and business-builder team. A balance on an app screen does not verify the claimed daily return or a completed withdrawal.

citations.quote: to generate the 1% profit per day
now do you see the BNB? This is your profits.
Only if you are sincere to join my team of investors and business builders then connect with me and I will guide you how.

opening.argument: There is an invitation to join a team and use an inviter link, so this should not be mistaken for neutral commentary. But a referral invitation is not, by itself, evidence of a fraudulent transaction. The description says joining is free and tells prospective investors to research the decision and risk only disposable income. In the supplied video, the speaker shows where a BNB amount appears in the app; that display does not establish that viewers have sent funds, that a withdrawal succeeded, or that anyone received the advertised daily return. Treat the referral as promotion requiring caution, without inferring those unshown outcomes.

do please do your own research and analysis before you embark on your own wealth creation journey. Invest ONLY the DISPOSABLE portion of your DISPOSABLE INCOME.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies a daily-return claim, recruitment language, and a withdrawal interface. Those are reasons for caution, but they do not establish that the displayed amount was paid out or that a viewer was induced to deposit. The creator says joining is free, and the description expressly conditions investing on the viewer's own research. The evidence supports a promotional referral with an unverified return claim; it does not show the completed transaction or outcome the opening itself says is missing.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Free enrollment does not make the promoted investment ordinary referral commerce. The creator invites viewers to join an investor team, supplies an inviter link, and describes lending cryptocurrency as generating 1% profit per day. The absence of a completed viewer deposit or withdrawal limits what can be concluded about outcomes, but it does not remove the investment-return pitch present in the video.
